Bond of Peace
BOND of PEES
n. phrase
Bond (Greek sundesmos, a binding, fastening) + peace (Greek eirēnē). Paul’s phrase in Ephesians 4:3: en tōi sundesmōi tēs eirēnēs, “in the bond of peace.”

📖 Biblical Definition

The bond of peace is Paul’s name for the active discipline by which the unity of the Spirit is preserved among the saints: a deliberate, sustained holding-together-in-peace that fastens believers to one another and keeps the Spirit-given oneness from being torn apart by the natural frictions of life-together. Ephesians 4:1-3 sets the doctrine in context: I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Several things stand together. First, the unity of the Spirit is given, not made: the Spirit Himself has constituted the one body, and the saints do not create unity but keep what He has given. Second, the keeping is active, not passive: endeavouring renders the Greek spoudazontes, “making every effort, being diligent”—the verb is intense, and the discipline is sustained. Third, the means is the bond of peace: the saints actively bind themselves to one another in the practice of peace, which Paul has just described as walking with all lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, and forbearance in love. The bond of peace is therefore not a vague spiritual sentiment but a concrete practice. It is constituted by the four virtues Paul names: lowliness (taking the lower seat, esteeming others better than self), meekness (the Spirit-shaped strength under control), longsuffering (the patience that bears with friction over time), and forbearing one another in love (the active letting-go of grievances and the willingness to overlook offenses). Where these four are practiced, the bond of peace holds, and the unity of the Spirit is preserved; where any of them fails, the bond strains, and the unity is threatened. Paul’s teaching has therefore both an indicative and an imperative dimension. Indicative: there is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Eph 4:4-6)—the unity is foundationally real and Spirit-given. Imperative: keep that unity, in the bond of peace, by the disciplined practice of the Christ-shaped virtues. The church saturated with the bond of peace is the church that demonstrates to the watching world the gospel-wrought reconciliation of saints who would otherwise be torn apart by natural frictions; the church that has lost the bond of peace is the church that fractures over what the bond of peace was given to absorb.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 treats bond as that which binds, fastens, or holds together, and peace as freedom from war or quarrel; Paul’s phrase bond of peace (Eph 4:3) names the active discipline by which the unity of the Spirit is preserved among the saints.

expand to see more

BOND, n. — 1. Anything that binds, as a cord, a chain, a rope; a band. 2. Ligament; that which holds things together. 3. Union; connection; a binding force or influence; cause of union; cement; that which unites or connects. Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph 4:3).

PEACE, n. — 1. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquility; freedom from disturbance or agitation. 2. Freedom from war with a foreign nation. 3. Freedom from internal commotion. 4. Concord; reconciliation between parties at variance. 5. In scripture, the spiritual peace of the soul reconciled to God in Christ, and the peace among the saints that flows from that reconciliation.

📖 Key Scripture

Ephesians 4:3 — "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace."

Ephesians 4:1-2 — "I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love."

Colossians 3:14-15 — "And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness. And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful."

Romans 12:18 — "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The bond of peace is corrupted, on one side, by the conflict-aversion register that mistakes peace-keeping at any cost for biblical peace—and on the other by the fractious-contention register that fractures the church over what the bond of peace was given to absorb, against Paul’s explicit endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit.

expand to see more

The conflict-aversion register mistakes peace-keeping at any cost for biblical peace. Faced with the friction of life-together, the conflict-averse saint avoids confrontation, suppresses concerns, declines to address sin, withdraws relationally rather than engaging difficulty—and calls this keeping the bond of peace. The bond of peace Paul describes is not this. Peace in Scripture is sometimes consistent with confrontation (Matt 18:15-17 commands confrontation precisely for the recovery of peace), with rebuke (Paul withstood Peter to his face for the sake of the gospel), and with the open address of sin (1 Cor 5; 2 Cor 7). The bond of peace is the active discipline of preserving Spirit-given unity by the practice of lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, and forbearance—not the suppression of all friction. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers the courage to address what needs addressing without losing the peace; the goal is not the absence of all confrontation but the sustained unity through whatever confrontations the love of Christ requires.

The opposite corruption is the fractious-contention register that fractures the church over what the bond of peace was given to absorb. Brothers report each other to elders for slight offenses; congregations split over secondary differences; networks of churches anathematize each other over matters Scripture has not made primary. The bond of peace Paul commands is precisely the absorbing of the ordinary frictions of fallen people loving one another in real time: the lowliness that does not need to be vindicated, the meekness that does not retaliate, the longsuffering that bears across time, the forbearance that overlooks what can be overlooked. Where these are practiced, the bond holds across enormous personal and theological diversity; where they fail, the bond breaks at the slightest provocation. Recover both ends. Refuse the conflict-aversion that mistakes silence for peace, and refuse the fractious contention that breaks the bond over what it was given to absorb. The church that practices the bond of peace as Paul means it is the church that demonstrates to the watching world the reconciliation only the gospel can produce.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sundesmos (a binding, fastening) + eirēnē (peace); Paul’s discipline of spoudazō (to make every effort) to keep the Spirit-given unity through the active practice of lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, and forbearance.

expand to see more

Greek sundesmos (G4886) — a binding together, fastening, bond (Eph 4:3; Col 2:19; 3:14; Acts 8:23).

Greek eirēnē (G1515) — peace (the great NT peace word; translates Hebrew shalom).

Greek spoudazō (G4704) — to make every effort, be diligent (Eph 4:3, “endeavouring”).

Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, completeness, soundness (the OT root of biblical peace).

Usage

"Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace—Paul names a Spirit-given unity actively preserved by the disciplined practice of Christ-shaped virtues."

"The bond of peace is constituted by lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, and forbearance—the four virtues of Ephesians 4:2."

"Conflict-aversion mistakes silence for peace; fractious contention breaks the bond over what it was given to absorb; biblical peace is sustained unity through whatever confrontations love requires."
